tagline: Open telemetry plus logs and security on one data store, not three Cisco SKUs
key_pain: AppDynamics is APM-only; customers still need Splunk or another tool for logs and SIEM. Cisco's portfolio (AppD, ThousandEyes, Splunk) is being stitched together but is not a single data plane today.

talking_points.claim: APM, logs, infra metrics, RUM and synthetics in one cluster, one query language.
talking_points.proof: Elastic APM ships service maps, distributed traces, RUM and synthetics natively. AppD requires bolt-ons (AppD plus Splunk plus ThousandEyes) for the equivalent footprint.

talking_points.claim: Native OTLP ingest plus the Elastic Distribution of OpenTelemetry Collector (EDOT).
talking_points.proof: AppD agents are proprietary; OTel support is partial and lags upstream. Customers re-instrumenting will not have to redo the work to leave Elastic.

talking_points.claim: One Elastic Agent ships logs, metrics, traces, security telemetry and endpoint signals.
talking_points.proof: AppD's Java/.NET/Node agents are application-only; you still need a separate log shipper and a separate SIEM agent.

elastic_advantages: OTel-native APM with no agent rewrite when tooling changes
Logs, metrics, APM, RUM, synthetics and Security in one license
Frozen tier on object storage for long traces and log retention
Self-hosted, Elastic Cloud, or hyperscaler marketplace deployment
Open ECS schema; no proprietary trace format lock-in

common_objections.q: AppDynamics Business iQ ties APM to revenue better than anything else.
common_objections.a: Business transactions can be modelled with Elastic APM custom labels plus Lens dashboards. Most customers we have migrated rebuild the 5 to 10 transactions that actually matter; the long tail of BiQ widgets goes unused.

common_objections.q: We are a Cisco shop; Splunk and AppD are now under one roof.
common_objections.a: They are under one roof on the org chart, not in the data plane. AppD and Splunk still bill separately, store data separately and require separate tooling. Elastic gives you one cluster today.

common_objections.q: AppD's auto-baselining and AI engine is more mature.
common_objections.a: Elastic ML jobs run unsupervised anomaly detection on any field, not just APM signals. Same engine works for log anomalies and security UEBA, which AppD does not cover.

common_objections.q: Migration risk on a tier-1 production application.
common_objections.a: Run AppD and Elastic APM agents in parallel on a single service; compare service maps and latency histograms; cut over by service, not by app.

discovery_questions: Where do your APM signals end and your logs/SIEM signals begin today, and how often do you need to pivot between them?
Are you on the Cisco bundle path or paying separately for AppD, ThousandEyes and Splunk?
How much of your APM agent footprint is OpenTelemetry today versus AppD proprietary?
What does your AppD renewal look like in the next 12 months?

tagline: Detection engineering depth and deployment flexibility Chronicle cannot match
key_pain: Chronicle (now Google Security Operations) is GCP-only at the data layer, has a closed UDM schema, and YARA-L is a steeper learning curve than customers expect. Hard to use outside Google Cloud.

talking_points.claim: Self-hosted, Elastic Cloud on AWS/GCP/Azure, or air-gapped on-prem.
talking_points.proof: Chronicle data lives in Google's tenant on GCP only. Regulated and multi-cloud customers (defence, healthcare, EU sovereignty) often disqualify it on residency alone.

talking_points.claim: Detection rules in KQL, EQL, ES|QL or Lucene; full Git-backed CI workflow via the detection engine API.
talking_points.proof: Chronicle's YARA-L 2.0 is powerful but proprietary; rule portability outside Chronicle is limited. Elastic detection rules are open-sourced in elastic/detection-rules on GitHub.

talking_points.claim: ECS is open and used by Beats, Agent and the wider OTel community.
talking_points.proof: Chronicle's UDM is proprietary and normalising third-party feeds requires Google parsers. ECS field mappings are public and editable.

elastic_advantages: Multi-cloud and on-prem deployment, not GCP-only
Open detection rule format with public Git repo
MITRE ATT&CK coverage with prebuilt detections plus a hunting workspace
Logs, observability and security on the same cluster
ELSER and inference API for semantic search on alerts and cases

common_objections.q: Chronicle's flat-rate ingest pricing is unbeatable for high-volume telemetry.
common_objections.a: True at the headline. The hidden costs are GCP egress when you query, parser engineering for non-Google sources, and the cost of being locked to GCP. Frozen tier on object storage closes most of the price gap on long retention.

common_objections.q: We already standardise on Google Cloud; Chronicle is the path of least resistance.
common_objections.a: Elastic Cloud runs on GCP with marketplace billing and PrivateLink equivalents. You keep the GCP relationship and gain multi-cloud optionality if the strategy ever changes.

common_objections.q: Chronicle's threat intel from VirusTotal is a real differentiator.
common_objections.a: Elastic's Threat Intel framework ingests VirusTotal, MISP, AlienVault OTX and any STIX/TAXII feed; enrichment runs at ingest or query time. Same intel, broader sourcing.

common_objections.q: The 12-month hot retention is a hard requirement we get for free in Chronicle.
common_objections.a: Elastic frozen tier on object storage gives 12+ months of searchable retention at object-storage prices. We can build the cost comparison side-by-side in the POV.

discovery_questions: Are any of your data sources outside GCP, and what does egress look like when SOC analysts query them?
How many of your detections are written in YARA-L versus inherited from Google curated rules?
Do you have any data residency or air-gap requirements that GCP-only deployment complicates?
How is Chronicle handling your non-security telemetry (observability, app logs)?

tagline: Cribl is a pipeline, not a destination. Elastic is the destination Cribl routes to.
key_pain: Cribl markets itself as 'reduce your SIEM bill 40 to 60 percent' by trimming low-value logs before they hit Splunk. The pitch only works because the destination is expensive. With Elastic, the storage economics make the pipeline savings less compelling, and Cribl adds another vendor and rule surface to maintain.

talking_points.claim: Cribl reduces ingest only because Splunk's ingest is expensive. Elastic's frozen tier removes the underlying cost driver, not the symptom.
talking_points.proof: If a customer is paying Cribl plus Splunk, they are paying twice to fix one pricing model. Elastic warm/cold/frozen tiers achieve similar TCO without an inline pipeline.

talking_points.claim: Routing, parsing, sampling and enrichment ship in the box.
talking_points.proof: Logstash filters, ingest node pipelines and Elastic Agent integrations cover route-to-multiple, drop, redact and sample. No separate Cribl Stream license required.

talking_points.claim: If the customer already runs Cribl, Elastic is happy to be a destination.
talking_points.proof: Cribl Stream has a native Elasticsearch destination; we recommend it for customers in mid-migration. The Cribl-versus-Elastic framing is not adversarial; we win the destination.

elastic_advantages: Frozen tier removes the cost driver Cribl was sold to fix
Ingest pipelines, Logstash and Elastic Agent processors cover most Cribl Stream use cases
Single vendor for collection, routing, storage and analytics
OTel Collector is the industry-direction pipeline; Elastic ships EDOT
Cribl Stream still works as a front-end if the customer prefers

common_objections.q: Cribl's routing UI is friendlier than YAML pipelines.
common_objections.a: Elastic Agent integrations are point-and-click in Fleet UI; Logstash pipelines are YAML but managed centrally. Most customers do not author new routing logic weekly; the UI gap is overstated.

common_objections.q: We already saved 40 percent on Splunk with Cribl. Why change?
common_objections.a: You can stack the savings: keep Cribl in front, migrate the destination to Elastic, and the frozen-tier economics compound. Or remove Cribl and go direct; both paths have a TCO model.

common_objections.q: Cribl Edge gives us OS-level collection without an agent footprint debate.
common_objections.a: Elastic Agent ships from a single binary across logs, metrics and security; footprint is well-documented. Cribl Edge is an alternative collector but not a meaningful differentiator on resource use.

discovery_questions: What is Cribl saving you against, in dollars, today?
If the destination cost dropped 60 percent, would the Cribl bill still be worth it?
Are you running Cribl Stream, Edge, or both, and who maintains the routing rules?
What is Cribl's renewal date and ARR?

tagline: Predictable storage economics plus open data for the AWS-heavy customer
key_pain: Per-host pricing plus index-rate ingest cost surprises. Vendor lock-in on the agent stack.

talking_points.claim: Pay for ingest plus storage tiers, not per-host. Frozen tier removes the index-rate trap.
talking_points.proof: Detailed cost calculator inline in our brief. Common 60 to 70 percent reduction at 18+ month retention.

talking_points.claim: First-party AWS marketplace billing, AWS PrivateLink ingest, IoT Core integration.
talking_points.proof: Same data plane handles factory edge telemetry plus cloud-native; Datadog requires separate IoT/Splunk-edge integration.

talking_points.claim: Logs, metrics, traces, and synthetics in one query language (ES|QL) and one data store.
talking_points.proof: Removes the Datadog notebook plus dashboard split that the customer is fighting today.

elastic_advantages: Storage cost predictability via warm/cold/frozen tiers
Open agent (Elastic Agent) avoids dd-agent vendor lock
OpenTelemetry-first; OTel Collector is GA
Native AWS Marketplace plus PrivateLink
Full-text search on logs (Datadog charges separately)

common_objections.q: Datadog APM is more refined for application teams.
common_objections.a: Elastic APM ships service maps, distributed traces, RUM, and synthetics. OTel-first means no agent rewrite when tooling changes.

common_objections.q: Datadog dashboards are easier to build.
common_objections.a: Kibana Lens is drag-and-drop; pre-built dashboards ship for common stacks (AWS, Kubernetes, Postgres). Vega for power users.

common_objections.q: Switching agents is too risky.
common_objections.a: Run dd-agent and Elastic Agent side-by-side during the POV. Cut over per service, not big-bang.

discovery_questions: What is your Datadog renewal date and current ARR with them?
Where does the ingest cost spike most: logs, traces, or custom metrics?

tagline: Open ecosystem and per-GB economics versus Dynatrace's DDU model
key_pain: Davis AI is genuinely strong on root-cause for traces, but DDU (Davis Data Unit) and DPS (Dynatrace Platform Subscription) pricing is opaque, and OneAgent is a heavyweight closed-source binary on every host.

talking_points.claim: Per-GB ingest plus storage tiering. No DDU/DPS unit translation.
talking_points.proof: Dynatrace customers consistently report DDU usage spikes after a major release; Elastic ingest cost is a flat $/GB and tiered storage is documented.

talking_points.claim: Elastic publishes EDOT (Elastic Distribution of OTel Collector) as a first-class agent.
talking_points.proof: Dynatrace OneAgent is closed-source. Their OTel ingest is supported but secondary; Davis only fully reasons over OneAgent data.

talking_points.claim: Lucene-backed log search on the same cluster as APM and metrics.
talking_points.proof: Dynatrace logs (Grail) is a separate data layer; query language (DQL) is Dynatrace-specific. Elastic uses ES|QL across all signals.

elastic_advantages: OTel-native; no proprietary agent lock-in
Logs, metrics, traces, RUM and synthetics on one cluster
Frozen tier for trace and log retention at object-storage prices
Self-hosted, Elastic Cloud, or hyperscaler marketplace
ML anomaly detection and ELSER included, not a separate SKU

common_objections.q: Davis AI's root-cause analysis is genuinely the best in APM.
common_objections.a: Davis is strong on traces; we will not pretend otherwise. Elastic ML covers anomaly detection across logs, metrics, traces and security signals; the wider scope wins for SecOps and platform teams. For pure APM RCA, scope the POV to that workflow specifically.

common_objections.q: OneAgent is install-once and discovers everything; Elastic Agent feels more manual.
common_objections.a: Elastic Agent has auto-discovery via Fleet integrations for Kubernetes, AWS services and 200+ sources. The gap exists but is narrow on common stacks.

common_objections.q: Dynatrace SaaS-only is fine, we are cloud-first.
common_objections.a: Elastic Cloud is fully managed too. The difference matters when a regulated workload, a new region, or an air-gap requirement appears later. Dynatrace Managed exists but is a separate product line.

common_objections.q: We have invested heavily in OneAgent rollout.
common_objections.a: Run EDOT/Elastic Agent on a subset of services first; OneAgent and OTel can co-exist on the same host. Migrate when the value is proven, not before.

discovery_questions: Where is your DDU consumption growing fastest, and is it predictable month over month?
How much of your instrumentation is OpenTelemetry today?
Are you using Dynatrace logs (Grail) or shipping logs elsewhere?
What is your Dynatrace renewal date and the current DPS commit?

tagline: UEBA without forcing a separate SIEM, plus open detection engineering
key_pain: Exabeam's UEBA is strong but the New-Scale platform consolidation has been rocky; many customers run Exabeam Fusion on top of another log source and pay twice. Smart Timelines are useful but proprietary.

talking_points.claim: Detection, investigation, response, UEBA and threat hunting on one cluster.
talking_points.proof: Elastic Security ships entity analytics (UEBA equivalent) plus the Timeline workspace, MITRE coverage and prebuilt detections. No separate UEBA SKU.

talking_points.claim: All detections are open-format; rules live in elastic/detection-rules on GitHub with full CI.
talking_points.proof: Exabeam detection content is proprietary; rule export is limited. Customers building a detection engineering practice keep ownership of their IP with Elastic.

talking_points.claim: Frozen tier on object storage at compliance-grade retention.
talking_points.proof: Exabeam Data Lake pricing scales with ingest; long retention is a recurring sore point. Elastic decouples ingest from storage cost via tiers.

elastic_advantages: Built-in entity analytics; no separate UEBA license
Open detection rule format on GitHub
MITRE ATT&CK navigator built into Kibana
Same platform serves observability use cases
Self-hosted, cloud, or air-gapped deployment

common_objections.q: Exabeam's Smart Timelines are unmatched for analyst experience.
common_objections.a: Elastic Timeline workspace gives analysts a similar pivoting experience with entity, host and process context. Worth scoping a side-by-side investigation in the POV; the gap is narrower than the marketing suggests.

common_objections.q: We have hundreds of Exabeam-tuned UEBA models.
common_objections.a: Elastic ML jobs cover the common UEBA patterns (rare process, unusual login geo, peer-group deviation) and are tunable per data view. Most customers consolidate to 20 to 30 high-signal models when migrating.

common_objections.q: Exabeam Fusion ingests our data already; switching disrupts SOC operations.
common_objections.a: Run dual-ingest during the POV; analysts work in both consoles for a month. Most decide based on case throughput, not theoretical features.

discovery_questions: Are you on classic Exabeam, Fusion, or the New-Scale platform, and how is the migration going?
How many of your detections are vendor-supplied versus authored by your team?
What is the ratio of UEBA license cost to total Exabeam ARR?
How is long-term retention handled today?

tagline: Co-exist on dashboards; win on the data layer
key_pain: Grafana the dashboard is loved by ops teams. Grafana the stack (Mimir, Loki, Tempo, Pyroscope) means three to four separate datastores to operate, and Grafana Cloud's pricing is metric-cardinality and active-series sensitive.

talking_points.claim: Mimir for metrics, Loki for logs, Tempo for traces, Pyroscope for profiling. Elastic does all four in one cluster.
talking_points.proof: Operating LGTM stack at scale requires four separate operational practices; Elastic consolidates to one cluster, one query language, one alerting layer.

talking_points.claim: Grafana is a great visualisation tool against Elasticsearch.
talking_points.proof: Elasticsearch is a first-class Grafana datasource. Customers who want Grafana dashboards keep them; Elastic wins the storage and query layer.

talking_points.claim: Loki's index-light design degrades on free-text search at scale.
talking_points.proof: Loki is optimised for label-based queries; ad-hoc investigations across TB/day datasets are slow. Lucene + ES|QL keep low-latency at production volumes.

elastic_advantages: Logs, metrics, traces and profiling on one cluster
Full-text search on logs without label engineering
MITRE ATT&CK Security workspace (Grafana stack has no SIEM)
Grafana datasource plugin keeps existing dashboards
Frozen tier for retention without sharding pain

common_objections.q: Grafana is open source; Elastic changed its license.
common_objections.a: Elastic moved core back to AGPLv3 in 2024 alongside ELv2; the OSS conversation has shifted. Both are usable in the OSI sense for the workloads our customers run. Worth grounding the conversation in the specific use case rather than the philosophical one.

common_objections.q: Loki's label model is cheap to operate.
common_objections.a: Cheap on storage, expensive on query when you need free-text or grep-equivalent search. Elastic's frozen tier matches Loki's storage model while keeping query depth.

common_objections.q: Mimir scales horizontally better than Elasticsearch for metrics.
common_objections.a: Elasticsearch metric ingest scales linearly with shards; downsampling and rollups close the gap on long retention. Mimir is genuinely strong for cardinality-heavy Prometheus, but most customers do not hit the crossover.

common_objections.q: We already have Grafana Cloud and a small platform team.
common_objections.a: Elastic Cloud is the parallel; same managed-service profile. The platform-team argument supports consolidation, not divergence.

discovery_questions: How many distinct Grafana data sources do you operate today, and who owns each?
Have you hit Loki's free-text search wall yet?
What is your active-series count on Mimir/Grafana Cloud?
Where does security telemetry live in the LGTM stack?

tagline: Same Lucene foundation, deeper analytics, real Security and ML
key_pain: Graylog runs on Elasticsearch or OpenSearch under the hood. Customers get a friendlier UI but inherit storage costs without warm/cold/frozen tiering, and Graylog's ML and SIEM features lag well behind Elastic Security.

talking_points.claim: Graylog is a UI on top of Elasticsearch/OpenSearch.
talking_points.proof: Going to Elastic directly removes a layer, unlocks frozen tier, native ML, ELSER and Elastic Security; Graylog Operations and Security plus Illuminate add cost without matching depth.

talking_points.claim: Object-storage retention without re-indexing.
talking_points.proof: Graylog requires manual archive/restore for old data; searchable snapshots in Elastic are queryable in place.

talking_points.claim: Public detection rules repo with hundreds of MITRE-mapped detections.
talking_points.proof: Graylog Illuminate content packs are smaller and updated less frequently. Detection engineering is an active discipline at Elastic.

elastic_advantages: Frozen tier on object storage
Native ML anomaly detection (no separate license)
Elastic Security with MITRE coverage
ELSER and inference API for semantic search
Open detection rules on GitHub

common_objections.q: Graylog is significantly cheaper.
common_objections.a: Headline-cheaper, especially in open core. Once Operations, Security and Illuminate licenses are added and you still need archive tooling, the gap narrows. Build the comparison at the customer's actual retention and feature footprint.

common_objections.q: Graylog's UI is simpler for our junior analysts.
common_objections.a: Kibana Discover and Lens are point-and-click. Where Graylog wins on simplicity it loses on depth (ML, Security workflows, ES|QL). Worth a hands-on with both.

common_objections.q: We already run Graylog on OpenSearch; switching is migration risk.
common_objections.a: OpenSearch and Elasticsearch share heritage but have diverged. A reindex from OpenSearch to Elasticsearch is documented; the bigger lift is rebuilding Graylog content packs as Elastic detections.

discovery_questions: Is your Graylog backed by Elasticsearch, OpenSearch, or MongoDB-only metadata?
How are you handling retention beyond 90 days today?
Which Graylog Enterprise modules (Operations, Security, Illuminate) are you paying for?
How much custom detection content has your team authored?

tagline: Wide-event observability with logs, metrics and security on the same cluster
key_pain: Honeycomb's event model and BubbleUp are excellent for high-cardinality debugging, but the platform is traces and events only. No logs, no metrics-as-first-class, no security. Customers buy Honeycomb plus another tool.

talking_points.claim: Honeycomb is APM-adjacent; Elastic covers logs, metrics, APM, RUM and Security.
talking_points.proof: Customers running Honeycomb almost always pair it with a separate log tool (Datadog, Splunk, or Elastic). Consolidating reduces the bill and the context-switch cost.

talking_points.claim: Both Honeycomb and Elastic are OTel-native; no instrumentation rewrite required.
talking_points.proof: Customers can ship OTel data to Elastic via OTLP; the EDOT distribution adds value-add processors. Same data, more destinations.

talking_points.claim: Elastic ML anomaly detection plus Lens 'top contributors' covers the high-cardinality slice analysis.
talking_points.proof: The workflow is different but the outcome is the same: identify which dimensions explain the anomaly. Worth a hands-on side-by-side.

elastic_advantages: Logs, metrics, APM and security on one cluster
OTel-native ingest with EDOT
Frozen tier for long event retention
ML anomaly detection across all signals
Self-hosted, cloud or air-gapped

common_objections.q: Honeycomb's BubbleUp is faster than anything else for high-cardinality root cause.
common_objections.a: On their core workflow, true. The question is whether the rest of the stack (logs, metrics, security) is worth the second tool. For pure SRE/dev teams that already have logs covered, Honeycomb may stay; for platform consolidation, Elastic wins.

common_objections.q: Honeycomb's query latency on wide events is sub-second.
common_objections.a: Elastic with hot-tier nodes hits sub-second on similar workloads. Worth benchmarking with the customer's actual queries during the POV.

common_objections.q: Our team likes the tracing-first mental model.
common_objections.a: Elastic APM has the same trace-first views (service map, distributed traces, dependencies). Discover and Lens are available when the team needs to leave the trace context.

discovery_questions: What other observability tools sit alongside Honeycomb today?
Is your team primarily SRE/dev or does Platform/Security need access too?
How are you handling logs and what is that bill?
How much of your Honeycomb spend is event volume versus retention?

tagline: Loki is cheap until you need to actually search
key_pain: Loki's index-light design (label index only, full-text grep at query time) is great for cost but punishing for ad-hoc investigations on TB/day workloads. LogQL is label-first; free-text and complex aggregations get slow.

talking_points.claim: Lucene + ES|QL maintain low-latency on free-text and aggregation queries at TB/day.
talking_points.proof: Loki regex queries scan all matching streams; performance degrades non-linearly with volume. Elastic's inverted index keeps median query latency in the hundreds of milliseconds at the same scale.

talking_points.claim: Frozen tier on object storage matches Loki's storage economics.
talking_points.proof: The Loki argument is 'cheap object-storage logs.' Elastic frozen tier is also S3/GCS/Azure Blob. The cost gap is smaller than positioning suggests; the query-quality gap is wider.

talking_points.claim: Same cluster handles metrics, traces, APM and Security.
talking_points.proof: Loki is logs-only by design; the LGTM stack stitches four products. Elastic consolidates.

elastic_advantages: Inverted index for low-latency free-text search
ES|QL aggregations across logs, metrics and traces
Frozen tier matches Loki's storage cost
ML anomaly detection on log fields
Security workspace on the same data

common_objections.q: Loki is the cheapest log store on the market.
common_objections.a: On ingest, often true. On total cost of ownership including the LGTM stack operations, search performance and the second tool needed for security, the gap narrows or inverts. Build the cost model at production scale, not pilot scale.

common_objections.q: We use LogQL because it matches PromQL; team mental model is consistent.
common_objections.a: ES|QL pipe syntax is similar to LogQL. The learning curve is one to two days for an engineer comfortable with LogQL.

common_objections.q: Loki labels keep our storage tiny.
common_objections.a: Until label cardinality explodes and Loki performance falls off. ECS plus Elastic's index-time mappings give predictable performance regardless of cardinality.

How often do analysts hit the 'this query timed out' wall?
What is the operational footprint of running Loki, Mimir, Tempo and Pyroscope?
Where does security telemetry live today?

tagline: Cloud-flexible SIEM without Azure lock-in or Log Analytics tax
key_pain: Sentinel's per-GB ingest pricing on Log Analytics is high once non-Microsoft sources arrive; data residency is Azure-only; KQL is Azure-specific; and the recent Defender XDR/Sentinel UI consolidation has been bumpy.

talking_points.claim: Self-hosted, AWS/GCP/Azure marketplace, or air-gapped.
talking_points.proof: Sentinel data lives in a Log Analytics workspace on Azure only; egress and cross-cloud customers pay heavily. Elastic Cloud runs on AWS, GCP and Azure with PrivateLink equivalents on each.

talking_points.claim: Sentinel pricing is friendly on Microsoft data, expensive on everything else.
talking_points.proof: Customers consistently report Sentinel costs spike when they add AWS CloudTrail, Okta, Crowdstrike or other non-Microsoft sources. Elastic per-GB pricing is uniform plus frozen tier removes long retention pain.

talking_points.claim: Detection rules are open and Git-managed; KQL detections are Azure-shaped.
talking_points.proof: Sentinel detections written in KQL bind the customer to Sentinel. Elastic detection rules are open-source on GitHub and portable.

elastic_advantages: Multi-cloud and on-prem deployment
Per-GB ingest with no Azure-source preference
Frozen tier on object storage at audit retention
Open detection rules on GitHub
Same platform handles observability, not just SIEM

common_objections.q: Defender XDR + Sentinel covers identity, endpoint and SIEM in one Microsoft story.
common_objections.a: It does for an all-Microsoft estate. The moment AWS, Okta, GCP, third-party endpoint or OT data arrives, the integration is shallower than the marketing suggests. Elastic Security handles the heterogeneous case.

common_objections.q: KQL is well-known to our analysts.
common_objections.a: ES|QL syntax is similar; pipe-style; Elastic also supports KQL for Kibana queries. The retraining cost is one to two weeks for an experienced KQL author.

common_objections.q: Microsoft has stronger threat intel from their telemetry.
common_objections.a: Microsoft's intel on Microsoft attack surface is genuinely strong. Elastic's Threat Intel framework integrates Microsoft, Mandiant, Recorded Future and any STIX/TAXII feed; you do not have to choose.

tagline: Predictable storage tiers versus New Relic's user-based plus ingest model

talking_points.claim: Elastic is OTel-native via EDOT.
talking_points.proof: New Relic supports OTel ingest but the differentiated experience still favours New Relic agents. Customers re-instrumenting on OTel keep optionality with Elastic.

talking_points.claim: Logs on the same cluster as APM; no Log Analytics add-on tier.
talking_points.proof: New Relic Logs counts toward the same data ingest pool but the analyst experience is APM-first. Elastic Discover is purpose-built for log investigation.

elastic_advantages: No per-user pricing on the platform
OTel-first via EDOT

Security workspace on the same cluster

tagline: Modern detection engineering and cloud deployment, not a 2010-era SIEM
key_pain: QRadar's appliance-and-EPS pricing model is a generation behind; AQL is proprietary and limited; IBM's pivot to QRadar Suite (with Cloud Pak) plus the AWS migration story is still settling. Many QRadar customers are already evaluating replacement.

talking_points.claim: Elastic Cloud is GA on AWS, GCP and Azure with marketplace billing.
talking_points.proof: QRadar on Cloud is hosted, but the architecture is still appliance-derived. EPS-based pricing makes capacity planning painful.

talking_points.claim: Open detection rules on GitHub; KQL/EQL/ES|QL/Lucene flexibility.
talking_points.proof: AQL is QRadar-specific and the rule engine is less flexible. Elastic detection rules are version-controlled and open-source.

talking_points.claim: Kibana plus the Security Solution workspace ship a modern hunting and investigation experience.
talking_points.proof: QRadar console is dated; pivot-to-context flows require multiple clicks. Elastic Timeline plus entity analytics consolidate the workflow.

elastic_advantages: Cloud-native deployment without appliance heritage
Per-GB pricing instead of EPS
Open detection rules and detection engineering CI
Frozen tier for compliance retention
Same platform handles observability

common_objections.q: QRadar is FedRAMP-authorised; we cannot move easily.
common_objections.a: Elastic Cloud has FedRAMP Moderate authorisation; self-managed Elastic in GovCloud also covers the workload. Check the customer's specific authority requirement.

common_objections.q: We have years of QRadar offences and content; rebuild is non-trivial.
common_objections.a: True; we plan a migration in phases. Elastic Security ships hundreds of prebuilt detections that cover the QRadar default content; custom rules port mechanically. Most QRadar customers find their truly differentiated content is 50 to 100 rules, not thousands.

common_objections.q: IBM is bundling QRadar Suite with Watson AI; that is a future bet worth waiting for.
common_objections.a: Possibly. The bet is unproven and the pricing is unclear. Elastic's ML and ELSER are GA today and included in the platform license.

common_objections.q: EPS pricing is what we know; switching to per-GB feels risky.
common_objections.a: Most QRadar customers undersize EPS and suffer dropped events. Per-GB is closer to what is actually flowing through the platform; we can model the conversion in the POV.

discovery_questions: Are you on QRadar appliance, on Cloud, or evaluating QRadar Suite?
What is your current EPS rating and how often do you hit it?
How many of your detections are IBM-supplied versus custom?
Is the IBM-to-Palo-Alto QRadar SaaS deal affecting your roadmap?

tagline: Cost-effective alternative for log analytics at audit-grade retention
key_pain: License plus storage costs are punitive at compliance retention windows. Index-time pricing scales linearly with ingest, not value.

talking_points.claim: Frozen tier on object storage cuts long-retention costs 60 to 80 percent.
talking_points.proof: Searchable snapshots on S3 / GCS / Azure Blob: pay storage rates, not warm-tier hot rates. Typical 18 month audit retention drops from $X to $X/4.

talking_points.claim: Logs, metrics, APM, and Security in one cluster on one license.
talking_points.proof: Eliminates Splunk Observability Cloud upsell + Splunk Enterprise Security add-on. Same data plane for ops + sec teams.

talking_points.claim: ECS plus Lucene index files are documented and exportable. No proprietary lock-in.
talking_points.proof: Customers can read raw index files; no vendor egress fee to leave Elastic.

elastic_advantages: Frozen tier on object storage at retention scale
Native cross-cluster search and replication included
Built-in ML anomaly detection (no separate license)
Open inference API for vector and sparse retrieval (ELSER)
Marketplace billing on AWS / GCP / Azure

common_objections.q: We have years of SPL queries; rewriting is a non-starter.
common_objections.a: ES|QL went GA in 8.13. SPL to ES|QL conversion docs are public; most queries map mechanically. Splunk-style pipe syntax is preserved.

common_objections.q: Splunk Enterprise Security is more mature for SIEM.
common_objections.a: Elastic Security ships MITRE ATT&CK coverage with prebuilt detections, plus a purpose-built threat-hunting workspace. Dashboarding parity since 8.x.

common_objections.q: Migration risk on a critical observability platform.
common_objections.a: Side-by-side dual-ingest period via Logstash or Filebeat outputs both targets. POV path validates parity before cutover.

discovery_questions: What is your audit retention requirement and what does the storage cost line look like today?
How many license tiers are you paying for across Splunk Core, Observability, and Enterprise Security?
If you had to consolidate to one platform in 12 months, what's the blocker?

tagline: Modern SIEM plus search depth Sumo cannot match
key_pain: Sumo's CSE is bolted on; query performance degrades at 100s of GB/day; cloud-only with no air-gap option.

talking_points.claim: Lucene indices plus dedicated search nodes hold low-latency at 1+ TB/day.
talking_points.proof: Customer benchmarks: median query latency 200ms at 2TB/day vs Sumo CSE 1.5s+.

talking_points.claim: Self-hosted, Elastic Cloud, AWS/GCP/Azure marketplace, plus air-gapped on-prem.
talking_points.proof: Sumo is SaaS-only; regulated workloads (defense, healthcare) often disqualify it.

talking_points.claim: Elastic Security ships MITRE ATT&CK coverage, entity analytics, and a hunting workspace.
talking_points.proof: Sumo CSE leans on rule packs; less customization at the detection-engineering layer.

elastic_advantages: Self-hosted plus cloud plus air-gapped
Full Lucene query depth at scale
MITRE ATT&CK + threat hunting in Security
Open Elastic Agent + Beats data shippers
ELSER for semantic search across logs

common_objections.q: Sumo is fully managed, less ops overhead.
common_objections.a: Elastic Cloud is fully managed too: hosted, patched, scaled. Same operational model with deeper search.

common_objections.q: We already trained the team on Sumo's query language.
common_objections.a: ES|QL syntax is similar; conversion docs exist; Lucene KQL also available for free-text users.

discovery_questions: Do you have any workloads that need air-gapped or self-hosted deployment?

Is your team feeling the limits of Sumo's CSE customization?

tagline: One data plane today versus a Cisco bundle that is still three products on three bills
key_pain: After Cisco closed the Splunk acquisition, the field pitch is 'AppDynamics for APM, ThousandEyes for network, Splunk for logs and SIEM, all under Cisco.' In reality the three platforms still have separate data stores, separate agents, separate billing models (DDU-style for AppD, ingest-based for Splunk Cloud, subscription for ThousandEyes) and the integration roadmap is public-but-vague. Customers buying the bundle today are buying a roadmap, not a unified product.

talking_points.claim: The Cisco bundle is three products with shared logos, not a shared data plane.
talking_points.proof: AppDynamics data lives in the AppD controller. Splunk data lives in Splunk indexers or Splunk Cloud. ThousandEyes data lives in the ThousandEyes SaaS. Cross-product correlation today goes through dashboard links and a planned 'unified experience,' not a shared store. Elastic has logs, metrics, APM, RUM, synthetics and Security on one cluster today.

talking_points.claim: Three pricing models stack instead of simplify.
talking_points.proof: AppDynamics is per-agent or DDU-equivalent; Splunk Cloud is workload pricing or ingest-based; ThousandEyes is per-test subscription. A typical enterprise bundle quote contains all three SKUs plus Cisco services attach. Elastic ships per-GB ingest plus storage tiers, one line item, frozen tier on object storage included.

talking_points.claim: Renewal cycles for AppD and Splunk now align under Cisco; that is the moment to evaluate.
talking_points.proof: Cisco is consolidating renewal calendars to make the bundle stickier. Customers who do not evaluate at this renewal will be locked in for another multi-year cycle. Run a focused POV on the highest-cost line (usually Splunk ingest or AppD agent count) before signing the bundle.

elastic_advantages: Single cluster for logs, metrics, APM, RUM, synthetics and Security
One per-GB ingest line plus storage tiers, no DDU or workload-pricing translation
OTel-native via EDOT; no proprietary agent stack to maintain
Frozen tier on object storage for compliance retention without bundle add-ons
Detection rules open-source on GitHub; not tied to Splunk ES or AppD content

common_objections.q: Cisco gave us a 30 percent bundle discount; the math is hard to beat.
common_objections.a: The discount is real but applied to three list prices that grew first. Build the comparison against actual usage, not list. In most deals we see, the bundle discount restores the price to roughly what each product cost separately two renewals ago.

common_objections.q: We are a Cisco networking shop; one throat to choke is valuable.
common_objections.a: True for support escalations. Less true for product roadmap: AppD, Splunk and ThousandEyes still have separate engineering orgs and separate release cycles. The single-vendor argument is operational, not technical.

common_objections.q: Splunk under Cisco will get cheaper over time.
common_objections.a: Possibly. The post-acquisition pattern across the industry is that prices flatten for two years and then resume the previous trajectory. Elastic gives you a real alternative now, not a hope on a roadmap.

common_objections.q: We need APM, network and logs; Elastic does not do network paths.
common_objections.a: Honest scope: ThousandEyes path-level network telemetry is its own niche. Most customers who buy the bundle use ThousandEyes for 5 to 10 critical paths. Keep ThousandEyes if it earns its keep; consolidate the rest to Elastic. Bundle pricing usually depends on all three products being on the contract, so this changes the negotiation.

discovery_questions: Are AppDynamics, Splunk and ThousandEyes on aligned renewal dates yet?
How is cross-product correlation working today: shared data, dashboard links, or manual?
What is the bundle uplift versus paying for each product separately?
Which of the three products would you keep if you could only keep one?

tagline: Dragos owns OT depth; Elastic is the SOC layer that surfaces OT signals to the business
key_pain: Dragos is genuinely best-in-class for OT and ICS threat detection: protocol-aware (Modbus, DNP3, IEC-61850, OPC-UA), industry-tuned threat groups (XENOTIME, ELECTRUM, CHRYSENE) and an air-gap-friendly deployment model. Elastic does not pretend to match Dragos at the OT-protocol depth layer. The real customer pain is that Dragos is OT-only: it does not cover IT, cloud, identity, endpoint or business systems. Customers running Dragos still need a SIEM for the rest of the enterprise, and OT alerts that never reach the IT SOC die in a separate console.

talking_points.claim: Elastic does not replace Dragos in the OT zone; Elastic is the SIEM that ingests Dragos alerts and correlates them with IT, identity and cloud telemetry.
talking_points.proof: Dragos exposes alerts and asset inventory via syslog, REST API and STIX/TAXII. Elastic Security ingests all three. The result: a converged IT/OT SOC view where an OT alert can be pivoted against the engineer's identity, the jump-host logs and the cloud control-plane events, all in one Timeline.

talking_points.claim: Dragos pricing scales with monitored assets and is rich for the depth it provides; layering Elastic underneath avoids paying Dragos prices for non-OT data.
talking_points.proof: Customers who try to use Dragos as their enterprise SIEM (because it is the security tool they have) end up overpaying for IT logs that do not need OT-protocol decoders. Elastic ingest economics on per-GB plus frozen tier are designed for the high-volume IT log layer.

talking_points.claim: Open detection rules on GitHub plus ML anomaly detection across IT and OT data.
talking_points.proof: Dragos detections are Dragos-authored and Dragos-distributed; that is fine for the OT zone. For the IT-OT correlation layer (where the breach actually moves) Elastic detection rules are open, version-controlled and auditable.

elastic_advantages: Full IT plus identity plus cloud plus endpoint coverage that Dragos does not attempt
Native ingest of Dragos alerts via syslog, REST and STIX/TAXII
Per-GB plus frozen tier economics for high-volume IT log retention
Open detection rules and ML anomaly detection across the converged dataset
Single SOC console for IT and OT analysts, with role-based access on the OT slice

common_objections.q: Dragos is the only platform that understands our OT protocols at depth.
common_objections.a: Agreed. Keep Dragos in the OT zone. The conversation is not Dragos versus Elastic; it is whether OT alerts ever reach the IT SOC. Today, in most plants, they do not. Elastic is the layer that closes that gap.

common_objections.q: We have an air-gapped OT network; cross-domain integration is hard.
common_objections.a: Common pattern: a one-way diode or guarded relay forwards Dragos alerts and asset inventory to the IT side. Elastic ingests on the IT side. The OT zone stays air-gapped; only the alert metadata crosses.

common_objections.q: Dragos has a SOC service offering too.
common_objections.a: Dragos OT Watch is for OT analysts. Most customers still need an enterprise SOC for IT and cloud. Elastic is the platform that SOC runs on; the two services are complementary.

common_objections.q: We do not want a second console for our OT team.
common_objections.a: OT analysts can stay in the Dragos console. The Elastic value is for the IT SOC and for IT-OT bridge investigations. Most plants we work with have separate analyst pools; the second console question only applies if the same analyst covers both.

discovery_questions: Where do Dragos alerts go today, and does the IT SOC see them?
What percentage of incidents started in IT and pivoted into OT, or the reverse?
Are you paying Dragos for asset coverage that is actually IT, not OT?
Who owns the IT-OT bridge: plant security, corporate SOC, or neither?

tagline: ServiceNow wins the SNOW-centric shop; Elastic wins on sovereignty, cost and ML
key_pain: ServiceNow ITOM (Discovery, Event Management, Health Log Analytics, Cloud Observability) is a credible observability and ITSM-adjacent monitoring story for customers who already run ServiceNow as their system of record. The honest tradeoff: data lives in the ServiceNow instance, pricing is subscription plus per-source plus per-event, log analytics depth is well behind purpose-built tools, and ML capabilities are early. Customers who are not already SNOW-centric pay a premium for the ITSM tie-in.

talking_points.claim: If the customer runs CMDB, change, incident and problem on ServiceNow, ITOM closes the loop on event-to-incident automation in a way no third party can.
talking_points.proof: Event Management plus the SNOW CMDB plus Flow Designer is genuinely the shortest path from alert to ticket to runbook for a SNOW-first shop. Elastic does not own the system of record; we integrate with it via the ServiceNow connector for cases and incidents.

talking_points.claim: Data sovereignty, cost at log scale, and ML maturity favour Elastic.
talking_points.proof: ITOM data lives in the ServiceNow instance with limited residency choice; Elastic deploys self-hosted, AWS/GCP/Azure marketplace or air-gapped. Health Log Analytics pricing scales with events; Elastic is per-GB plus frozen tier. Elastic ML anomaly detection and ELSER are GA; ServiceNow Predictive AIOps is newer and narrower.

talking_points.claim: Most enterprises end up running both: Elastic for the data plane, ServiceNow for the ITSM workflow.
talking_points.proof: Elastic Cases integrate with ServiceNow incidents bidirectionally. The customer keeps SNOW for change and incident; Elastic owns logs, metrics, APM and Security. This is the dominant pattern in regulated and multi-cloud accounts.

elastic_advantages: Self-hosted, multi-cloud or air-gapped deployment versus SNOW-instance-only
Per-GB plus frozen tier economics at log retention scale
Mature ML anomaly detection and ELSER inference in the platform
Open detection rules and Security workspace on the same cluster
Bidirectional ServiceNow connector preserves the ITSM workflow

common_objections.q: ITOM Visibility plus the CMDB is unmatched for ITSM-driven ops.
common_objections.a: Agreed for the ITSM workflow. The question is whether ITOM is the right place to store the underlying telemetry. Most customers we work with keep SNOW as the system of record and put the data plane elsewhere; the integrations are mature.

common_objections.q: Health Log Analytics gives us logs inside ServiceNow.
common_objections.a: It does, at SNOW pricing and with SNOW search depth. For a few-hundred-GB-per-day shop it works. Past 1 TB per day or with deep ad-hoc query needs, the economics and the query latency push customers to a purpose-built log platform.

common_objections.q: We want one vendor for ITSM and observability.
common_objections.a: Reasonable goal. The single-vendor argument trades flexibility for simplicity. Worth modelling cost at the customer's actual ingest and the analyst experience for log search; the gap is wider than the marketing suggests.

common_objections.q: Predictive AIOps will catch up to Elastic ML.
common_objections.a: Possibly over time. Today, Elastic ML jobs cover anomaly detection on any field, support forecasting, and feed Security UEBA on the same engine. Predictive AIOps is event-clustering-first and narrower. Build the comparison on real customer data.

discovery_questions: Is ServiceNow your system of record for incident and change today?
What is your daily log ingest, and is Health Log Analytics handling all of it?
Do you have data residency or air-gap requirements that the ServiceNow instance complicates?
Where does Security telemetry live, and is it in scope for ITOM?

tagline: Workload pricing plus egress: Splunk Cloud trades one cost surprise for another
key_pain: Splunk Cloud is not just hosted Splunk Enterprise; it is a different commercial and operational model. Workload pricing (SVC) replaces ingest-based pricing for most new customers, which can be friendlier for predictable workloads and punishing for spiky ones. Data lives in AWS or GCP regions chosen by Splunk, and querying from outside that region surfaces egress and latency costs the customer did not have on-prem. Long retention still pushes customers to SmartStore plus a separate object-storage bill, and the Splunk Cloud admin surface is narrower than Splunk Enterprise.

talking_points.angle: Workload pricing is not a free lunch
talking_points.claim: SVC pricing is good for steady-state ingest and bad for spike-heavy workloads.
talking_points.proof: Splunk SVC is sized to peak compute. A monthly close, a holiday traffic surge or an incident-driven query burst forces a higher SVC tier for a year. Elastic per-GB ingest plus auto-scaling on Elastic Cloud handles spikes without re-tiering the contract.

talking_points.claim: Splunk Cloud regions are limited; querying across regions or pulling data out incurs cost and latency.
talking_points.proof: Splunk Cloud Platform has a fixed regional footprint per cloud. Cross-region search is constrained. Elastic Cloud runs in 50+ regions on AWS, GCP and Azure with PrivateLink and VPC peering on each.

talking_points.claim: Splunk Cloud SmartStore puts cold data on S3, but the warm-tier SVC still drives the bill.
talking_points.proof: Frozen tier on Elastic uses object storage and remains queryable in place via searchable snapshots. The economics for 12 to 24 month retention are typically 50 to 70 percent lower than the equivalent Splunk Cloud SVC plus storage line.

elastic_advantages: Per-GB ingest plus elastic auto-scaling handles spikes without re-tiering
Multi-cloud regional footprint with native PrivateLink and VPC peering
Frozen tier on object storage at retention scale
ES|QL and SPL-to-ES|QL conversion docs lower migration friction
Same platform owns logs, metrics, APM and Security on one license

common_objections.q: Splunk Cloud is fully managed; we have no ops overhead.
common_objections.a: Elastic Cloud is fully managed too: hosted, patched, auto-scaled. Same operational profile, broader regional choice, and per-GB pricing instead of SVC.

common_objections.q: SVC pricing is finally predictable; we know the bill.
common_objections.a: Predictable until a spike forces a tier change at renewal. SVC is right-sized to peak, so the bill reflects the worst week, not the average. Elastic ingest economics track usage.

common_objections.q: Our data has to stay in a specific region; Splunk Cloud covers it.
common_objections.a: Confirm the exact region. Splunk Cloud regional coverage is narrower than the hyperscalers. Elastic Cloud usually has more options, including air-gapped self-hosted on FedRAMP or sovereign clouds.

common_objections.q: We have years of SPL and dashboards; rewriting is a non-starter.
common_objections.a: ES|QL went GA in 8.13 with a documented SPL-to-ES|QL conversion path. Most queries port mechanically; dashboards are rebuilt in Lens with Vega for the complex cases. POV scope: rebuild the top 20 dashboards and 50 detections, validate parity, then commit.

discovery_questions: Are you on workload (SVC) pricing or legacy ingest-based pricing?
How spiky is your ingest pattern, and how does that interact with SVC sizing?
Are your analyst and ingest regions aligned with the Splunk Cloud regions you can choose?
What is your retention requirement, and how is SmartStore plus warm-tier costed today?

tagline: Wiz owns CSPM and cloud config-vuln graph; Elastic is the SIEM beneath it
key_pain: Wiz is genuinely best-in-class for cloud security posture management, agentless cloud workload scanning, and the graph-based correlation of misconfigurations, vulnerabilities, identities and exposed assets across AWS, Azure, GCP and Kubernetes. Elastic does not match Wiz at the cloud-config-and-vuln correlation layer and should not pretend to. The customer pain is that Wiz is a posture and findings platform, not a SIEM: it does not store endpoint logs, identity logs, network logs at SOC retention, and alerting on Wiz findings still needs a SIEM to drive incident workflow and long retention.

talking_points.claim: Wiz finds cloud posture risk; Elastic Security is the SIEM that ingests Wiz findings, correlates them with runtime signals, and runs the SOC workflow.
talking_points.proof: Wiz exposes findings via webhook, REST API and the Wiz Issues integration. Elastic ingests all three and runs detection rules that correlate Wiz issues with CloudTrail, GuardDuty, EDR and identity logs. The combined pattern (Wiz plus Elastic) is the dominant deployment for cloud-mature customers we see.

talking_points.claim: Long retention, SIEM-tier correlation across non-cloud data, and open detection engineering.
talking_points.proof: Wiz retains findings for the policy window; SOC investigation needs months of raw log retention which Wiz does not store. Elastic frozen tier keeps full logs queryable for 12+ months. Elastic detection rules cover identity, endpoint, network and cloud, not just cloud posture.

talking_points.claim: Agentless cloud scanning and graph-based blast-radius analysis are Wiz strengths.
talking_points.proof: Wiz Security Graph correlates misconfig plus vuln plus identity plus exposure in a way that is purpose-built and well-tuned. Elastic does not replace this layer; we integrate with it. Honest scoping wins more deals than feature parity claims.

elastic_advantages: SIEM-tier log retention and correlation that Wiz does not provide
Native ingest of Wiz findings via webhook and REST API
Detection rules across identity, endpoint, network and cloud, not posture-only
Frozen tier on object storage for 12+ months of queryable retention
Same platform owns logs, metrics, APM and Security on one license

common_objections.q: Wiz already gives us a security view; do we need a SIEM?
common_objections.a: Wiz gives you a posture view. A SIEM gives you the runtime view, the long-retention investigation surface, and the cross-domain correlation. Most customers buy both; the question is which SIEM, not whether to have one.

common_objections.q: Wiz Defend is becoming a runtime detection platform too.
common_objections.a: Wiz Defend is real and growing; it focuses on cloud-runtime detection. It is not a general-purpose SIEM and does not own identity, endpoint or network telemetry at scale. The boundary is moving but the SIEM gap remains for now.

common_objections.q: We are buying SIEM-tier; can Elastic do CSPM too?
common_objections.a: Honest answer: Elastic has cloud security posture features through the Cloud Security integration, but Wiz is deeper at the graph correlation layer. If the customer is buying SIEM-tier and accepts good-enough CSPM, Elastic alone can fit. If the customer wants best-in-class CSPM, Wiz plus Elastic is the right pattern.

common_objections.q: Two vendors means two consoles for the SOC.
common_objections.a: Wiz issues land in Elastic Cases; analysts work the case in Elastic with full enrichment and retention. Wiz remains the source of truth for posture; Elastic is the workflow surface. Most SOCs prefer this split.

discovery_questions: Where do Wiz findings go today: ticketing, SIEM, email?
What is your SOC log retention requirement, and is Wiz storing that data?
Are you buying SIEM-tier, posture-tier, or both?
How are runtime cloud detections handled today: Wiz Defend, GuardDuty, EDR, or SIEM rules?

tagline: Same Lucene roots, but Elastic ships the platform features OpenSearch lacks
key_pain: AWS OpenSearch is a 7.10 fork that has diverged on plugins, ML, vector and APM. Customers picking it for AWS-native billing inherit a slower release cadence, no semantic_text, and no first-party APM or SIEM workflow. The community is real but smaller and AWS-centric.

talking_points.claim: ELSER, semantic_text, ES|QL, Universal Profiling, APM and Elastic Security exist in Elastic and not in OpenSearch.
talking_points.proof: OpenSearch ML Commons covers vector and a subset of NLP, but there is no semantic_text mapping, no ELSER sparse model, and no full APM/Security UI. Compare release notes side by side.

talking_points.claim: Elastic ships major capability every 6 to 8 weeks; OpenSearch tracks AWS service rhythms.
talking_points.proof: Vector quantization (BBQ), inference API, ES|QL and Search Applications shipped in Elastic in 2024 and 2025; OpenSearch parity lags by quarters or has no equivalent.

talking_points.claim: Elastic Cloud runs on AWS, GCP and Azure with marketplace billing on all three.
talking_points.proof: OpenSearch Service is AWS only. Multi-cloud or on-prem regulated customers default-disqualify it on residency.

elastic_advantages: ELSER and semantic_text for built-in semantic search with no model wrangling
ES|QL piped query language plus EQL for security analytics
First-party APM, RUM, synthetics and Elastic Security on the same cluster
Universal Profiling for whole-fleet eBPF flame graphs
Frozen tier on S3 with searchable snapshots integrated and supported
Multi-cloud deployment (AWS, GCP, Azure) and on-prem or air-gapped

proof_points.metric: ELSER and semantic_text shipped GA in Elastic 8.11; no equivalent in OpenSearch.
Better Binary Quantization (BBQ) reduces vector RAM by ~32x with minimal recall loss.
Elastic ships APM, RUM, Profiling and Security on the same data plane; OpenSearch ships none of these.

objection_handlers.q: We are AWS-only and OpenSearch is one click in the console.
objection_handlers.a: Elastic Cloud on AWS is also one click via AWS Marketplace, with PrivateLink and consolidated billing. You keep AWS-native procurement and gain the platform features OpenSearch is missing.

objection_handlers.q: OpenSearch is open source; Elastic relicensed under ELv2 and SSPL.
objection_handlers.a: Elastic is back to AGPLv3 since 2024 and is OSI-recognised again. The OpenSearch fork was created under different conditions; the licensing argument has expired.

objection_handlers.q: Our team already knows the OpenSearch dashboard and APIs.
objection_handlers.a: OpenSearch and Elastic share the 7.10 API surface. ES|QL is additive and Kibana feature parity is high. Migration cost is mostly index reconfiguration, not query rewriting.

pricing_anchor: AWS OpenSearch Service on-demand from ~$0.036/hr for t3.small.search; production tiers scale per node hour plus EBS plus data transfer. See aws.amazon.com/opensearch-service/pricing.
gotchas: OpenSearch is materially cheaper for a write-once log archive on small clusters.
AWS-native shops with deep IAM integration get tighter Cognito/IAM auth out of the box on OpenSearch Service.
OpenSearch Dashboards (forked Kibana) is good enough for basic log search; the gap shows in APM, Security and ML, not in raw search.
OpenSearch has its own Anomaly Detection plugin; for simple metric anomalies it is comparable.
discovery_questions: Are you on OpenSearch Service or self-managed OpenSearch, and on what version?
What use cases are you running today: logs, search, vectors, security, or all of the above?
Have you hit any of the missing features: ELSER, semantic_text, ES|QL, APM, Security?
Is multi-cloud or on-prem on the 24-month roadmap, or is AWS-only locked in?
Who owns the OpenSearch cluster operationally, and what is the on-call burden?
clincher: Same engine origin, but Elastic kept building the platform; OpenSearch kept building the AWS console integration.

tagline: Stop running two databases. BM25 plus dense plus ELSER under one query.
key_pain: Pinecone is a vector-only managed service. Customers pair it with Elastic, Postgres or another keyword store for hybrid search, then pay for both, sync data both ways and reconcile two ranking models at query time. The architecture is simple until you need filters, full text or audit retention.

talking_points.claim: BM25, dense vectors and ELSER sparse retrieval combine in a single _search call with rank-fusion (RRF) built in.
talking_points.proof: Pinecone added sparse-dense hybrid in 2024 but you still need a separate BM25 index for production keyword relevance. Elastic ranks all three together with reciprocal rank fusion.

talking_points.claim: Pre-filter and post-filter on hundreds of metadata fields; nested documents and security filters supported.
talking_points.proof: Pinecone metadata filtering exists but performance falls off on high-cardinality filters. Elastic was designed for filtered search from day one.

talking_points.claim: The same cluster can serve RAG, log analytics, observability and security search.
talking_points.proof: Customers consolidate to one license and one operations surface. Pinecone solves vectors only; everything else is somebody else's bill.

elastic_advantages: Hybrid BM25 plus dense plus ELSER with built-in RRF
ELSER (sparse) gives strong out-of-domain retrieval with no fine-tuning
BBQ vector quantization for cost-efficient memory at scale
Native data ingestion, parsing and enrichment without an ETL service
Searchable snapshots on object storage for cheap long-term vector retention
Self-hosted, Elastic Cloud and air-gapped deployment options

proof_points.metric: Elastic supports dense, sparse (ELSER) and BM25 hybrid via RRF in one query (8.8+).
BBQ delivers ~95% recall at ~1/32 the memory of float32 vectors.
Pinecone Standard is $0.096/hr per p1.x1 pod plus storage. Two databases means two bills.

objection_handlers.q: Pinecone has the lowest p99 vector latency we have seen.
objection_handlers.a: True at the dedicated-vector tier and at extreme query rates. For mixed workloads with filters, BM25 and reranking, Elastic typically wins on end-to-end relevance latency because there is no second hop and no client-side fusion.

objection_handlers.q: Pinecone is fully managed; we do not want to run a search cluster.
objection_handlers.a: Elastic Cloud Serverless gives you the same managed surface: pay for ingest plus search, no node sizing. The vector tier is autoscaled.

objection_handlers.q: Our team already wired Pinecone into LangChain and LlamaIndex.
objection_handlers.a: Both frameworks ship a first-class Elasticsearch retriever. The migration is a connection-string change plus an index mapping; data backfill runs from your source of truth.

pricing_anchor: Pinecone Starter is free; Standard pods at ~$0.096/hr per p1.x1 plus storage. See pinecone.io/pricing for current tiers.
gotchas: On a pure-vector workload at very high QPS, Pinecone serverless can be cheaper and simpler to operate.
Pinecone's namespaces give effortless multi-tenant isolation; Elastic uses index-per-tenant or document-level security, which is more flexible but more setup.
Pinecone has a smaller, simpler API surface that some teams prefer for prototype RAG apps.
Pinecone serverless billing is decoupled from infrastructure; very bursty workloads can land cheaper there.
discovery_questions: Beyond vectors, where else does the search live today: BM25, Postgres FTS, Algolia, or somewhere else?
How many metadata filters does each query carry, and what is the cardinality?
What is your Pinecone bill at peak month, and is it growing linearly with corpus or with QPS?
Do you reconcile two ranking models in application code today, or do you let Pinecone do it all?
What is the freshness SLA between source of truth and the vector index?
clincher: Pinecone is a vector cache. Elastic is the search engine your data already lives in.

tagline: Vector-native works until you need keyword, filters and security on one cluster
key_pain: Weaviate is a clean, vector-native open source database with strong GraphQL ergonomics. It is a great fit for greenfield RAG. Where it strains: enterprise auth, large filtered queries, hybrid scoring beyond a single index, and operational features that Elastic shipped a decade ago.

talking_points.claim: Elastic combines BM25, dense vectors and ELSER sparse with RRF; Weaviate hybrid is BM25 plus dense only.
talking_points.proof: ELSER outperforms BM25 on out-of-domain corpora without fine-tuning and stacks with dense vectors via RRF in one Elastic query.

talking_points.claim: Tiered storage, snapshot-restore, cross-cluster search and ILM are mature in Elastic.
talking_points.proof: Weaviate has snapshots and replication but lacks the warm/cold/frozen pattern, cross-cluster search and policy-driven lifecycle that regulated customers depend on.

talking_points.claim: Vectors, logs, metrics, traces and security on one cluster with one auth model.
talking_points.proof: Weaviate is a vector DB. Bringing in observability or SIEM means standing up another stack.

elastic_advantages: BM25 plus dense plus ELSER hybrid with RRF in one query
Document-level security and field-level security built in
Frozen tier on object storage for cold vector retention
Native ingest pipelines, no separate ETL service required
Same cluster runs observability and security workloads
AGPLv3 open source plus commercial support and Elastic Cloud

proof_points.metric: Elastic ships ELSER sparse retrieval; Weaviate uses BM25 for the sparse leg of hybrid.
Elastic 8.x supports document-level and field-level security on vector indices.
Searchable snapshots store cold data on S3/GCS/Azure Blob at object-storage prices.

objection_handlers.q: Weaviate has GraphQL out of the box; our app team prefers it.
objection_handlers.a: Elastic exposes a typed REST API plus client libraries that most LLM frameworks already integrate. If GraphQL is a hard requirement, a thin gateway in front of Elastic is a 1-day build.

objection_handlers.q: Weaviate's class schema and modules feel cleaner than Elastic mappings.
objection_handlers.a: Mappings carry more responsibility because Elastic indexes structured logs, metrics and security events too. For a pure vector use case the schema delta is small.

objection_handlers.q: Weaviate is open source and we want to self-host.
objection_handlers.a: Elastic is open source under AGPLv3 and ships a self-managed binary with no telemetry or phone-home. Same self-host story, much wider feature surface.

pricing_anchor: Weaviate Cloud Standard tier starts around $25/month for small workloads; production workloads price per dimension and stored object. See weaviate.io/pricing for current tiers.
gotchas: For a pure RAG prototype with no other data, Weaviate is faster to stand up than tuning an Elastic mapping.
Weaviate's vectorizer modules (text2vec-openai, text2vec-cohere) are convenient; Elastic uses the inference API which is comparable but newer.
Weaviate has a friendlier developer story for engineers who only ever want vectors and modules.
If you do not care about logs, metrics, traces or security telemetry, the platform breadth is wasted.
discovery_questions: What is on the same data plane as your vectors today, and what is on a different stack?
Are you running keyword (BM25) somewhere alongside Weaviate, and how is that bill split?
Do you have document-level access control needs (per-customer, per-tenant)?
What does your retention story look like for cold vectors after 6 months?
Where is the renewal pressure: Weaviate Cloud, the keyword side, or both?
clincher: Pick Weaviate if you only ever need vectors. Pick Elastic when search is a platform decision.

tagline: Billion-scale vectors are useful; the question is what else lives on the same cluster
key_pain: Milvus and Zilliz Cloud lead pure-vector benchmarks at billion-scale and offer GPU indexing. The tradeoff is operational complexity (etcd, Pulsar, MinIO components) and a narrow feature set: no first-class BM25, weak metadata filtering performance, no observability or security workloads on the same cluster.

talking_points.claim: Elastic combines BM25, dense vectors and ELSER sparse via RRF in one query; Milvus hybrid is dense plus a basic sparse vector.
talking_points.proof: ELSER plus BM25 plus dense in one ranked result set is a single Elastic query. Milvus achieves similar scoring with two collections and client-side fusion.

talking_points.claim: Elastic ships as one binary plus optional Kibana; Milvus depends on etcd, Pulsar/Kafka and an object store.
talking_points.proof: The Milvus distributed deployment is documented to require multiple services; Zilliz Cloud abstracts this for a price. Elastic Cloud is a single managed surface.

talking_points.claim: Same cluster serves search, logs, observability and security; one license, one ops model.
talking_points.proof: Customers replace 3-4 single-purpose tools with Elastic. Milvus does vectors well and only vectors.

elastic_advantages: BM25 plus dense plus ELSER hybrid in one ranked query (RRF)
BBQ vector quantization for low memory cost at billion scale
Single-process deployment with native scaling, no etcd/Pulsar dependency
Searchable snapshots on object storage for cold vectors
Mature multi-tenant security (DLS, FLS, API keys, SSO)
Same cluster handles logs, metrics, traces and security telemetry

proof_points.metric: BBQ reduces vector RAM by ~32x with minimal recall loss versus float32.
Elastic supports billion-scale vector indices with HNSW and tiered storage.
Elastic 8.x ships ELSER sparse retrieval with no fine-tuning required.

objection_handlers.q: Milvus benchmarks higher QPS on pure vector at billion scale.
objection_handlers.a: On a pure-vector benchmark with no filters, no BM25 and no auth, Milvus can win. Production workloads almost always carry filters, security and BM25; the head-to-head numbers shift quickly.

objection_handlers.q: Milvus has GPU indexing, Elastic does not.
objection_handlers.a: True today. Elastic ships HNSW with BBQ on CPU and remains competitive at billion scale; the GPU advantage is mostly index build time, not query latency.

objection_handlers.q: We standardised on open source; Milvus is Apache 2.0.
objection_handlers.a: Elastic is back to AGPLv3 OSI-recognised open source as of 2024. Both are open source; the platform breadth is the differentiator now.

pricing_anchor: Milvus is free open source; Zilliz Cloud Serverless is usage-based starting around $0.10 per million vectors per hour. See zilliz.com/pricing.
gotchas: Milvus is the right choice when the entire architecture is pure vector at very high scale and nothing else.
GPU index build is genuinely faster on Milvus for huge corpora rebuilt frequently.
Zilliz Cloud has a clean, vector-only console that some teams prefer to Kibana for RAG-only work.
Milvus 2.4+ has a cleaner partition-key story for very high-cardinality multi-tenant vector apps.
discovery_questions: What is the corpus size today, what will it be in 12 months, and how often is it fully rebuilt?
How many filters, ACLs or tenants does each query carry?
Do you also need keyword search, and if so where does it live today?
Who runs the Milvus cluster operationally and what is the on-call burden?
What other workloads sit next to vector search: logs, observability, security?
clincher: Milvus stores vectors. Elastic powers the application that uses them.

tagline: Great for one site search. Elastic is the platform for everything that comes after.
key_pain: Typesense is fast to install, has a clean API and a generous free tier, and makes site search trivial. The ceiling appears the moment you need: enterprise auth, multi-cluster, security analytics on the same data, log retention, or anything beyond product-search ranking.

talking_points.claim: Elastic grows with the customer from site search to observability, security and AI Search.
talking_points.proof: Customers consolidate from 3-4 vendors to one Elastic license; Typesense remains a single-purpose tool.

talking_points.claim: BM25 plus dense plus ELSER sparse with RRF in one ranked result set.
talking_points.proof: Typesense supports dense vectors and BM25 hybrid; ELSER sparse retrieval and RRF rank fusion are Elastic-only.

talking_points.claim: RBAC, document-level security, SSO/SAML/OIDC, audit log and FedRAMP options ship in Elastic.
talking_points.proof: Typesense API keys are scoped well for one app; multi-team enterprise governance and compliance certifications are limited.

elastic_advantages: BM25 plus dense plus ELSER hybrid scoring with RRF
Document-level and field-level security for multi-tenant catalogs

ELSER plus BM25 plus dense via RRF outperforms BM25-only on retrieval recall.
Elastic Behavioral Analytics tracks query reformulation, click-through and conversion natively.

objection_handlers.q: Typesense was running in 30 minutes; Elastic feels like more setup.
objection_handlers.a: Elastic Cloud Serverless gets to the same first-query speed; the apparent gap is mostly tutorial polish. The investment pays back when the second use case (logs, security, vectors) reuses the same cluster.

objection_handlers.q: Typesense's typo tolerance is unbeatable out of the box.
objection_handlers.a: Elastic ships fuzziness AUTO plus phonetic and edge n-gram tokenizers; tuning takes a half day for the same result. The default is less aggressive on purpose to control recall.

objection_handlers.q: We do not need observability or security; site search is the only use case.
objection_handlers.a: Then Typesense is a defensible choice today. The question is the 24-month roadmap: most product teams add personalization, A/B testing or analytics, and Elastic scales into that without a re-platform.

pricing_anchor: Typesense Cloud starts around $25/month for a small node; production clusters scale per node hour. See typesense.org/pricing.
gotchas: For a single-page e-commerce or docs site search, Typesense is faster to ship and cheaper at small scale.
Typo tolerance defaults are friendlier without tuning; Elastic requires a few minutes of analyzer config to match.
Typesense's developer experience and documentation are excellent for greenfield apps.
Curation rules are simpler in Typesense for non-engineers than in Elastic Search Applications.
discovery_questions: What other data lives in Typesense today, and what does not?
Is multi-region or multi-tenant on the roadmap, and what does that look like in Typesense?
Do you have personalization, A/B test or boost-by-business-rules requirements coming?
What is the analytics story for search KPIs (click-through, conversion, abandonment)?
Where does observability and security data live today, and is consolidation on the table?
clincher: Typesense ends at site search. Elastic begins there.

tagline: Developer-friendly is great until the security team and the SRE team show up
key_pain: Meilisearch is the most loved developer experience in the search space: a single binary, instant install, JS-first SDKs, prefix search and typo tolerance enabled by default. The ceiling appears around enterprise scale: limited multi-tenant security, no tiered storage, no first-party observability, no SIEM workflow.

talking_points.claim: Elastic ships BM25 plus dense plus ELSER sparse with RRF; Meilisearch hybrid is BM25 plus dense.
talking_points.proof: ELSER sparse retrieval and three-way RRF rank fusion are Elastic-only. Meilisearch added vectors in v1.6 (2024) but the hybrid surface is narrower.

talking_points.claim: Document-level security, field-level security, SSO/SAML/OIDC, audit log and FIPS deployment ship in Elastic.
talking_points.proof: Meilisearch tenant tokens are scoped well for an app; corporate IAM, audit and compliance certifications are limited.

talking_points.claim: Same cluster runs site search, RAG, observability and security.
talking_points.proof: Meilisearch is search-only by design. Elastic replaces 3-4 single-purpose stacks at consolidation time.

objection_handlers.q: Meilisearch was running in 5 minutes and the JS client is beautiful.
objection_handlers.a: Elastic Cloud Serverless plus the Search Application client closes most of the gap; the first-experience polish is real but the long-term ceiling matters more for the team you support 24 months out.

objection_handlers.q: Typo tolerance defaults are friendlier in Meilisearch.
objection_handlers.a: True out of the box. Elastic ships fuzziness AUTO and the new lexical and semantic relevance defaults; tuning matches Meilisearch in a few hours.

objection_handlers.q: We are JavaScript-first; Elastic feels Java-centric.
objection_handlers.a: The official @elastic/elasticsearch JS client is mature and TypeScript-typed. The internals are Java; the developer surface is HTTP plus a clean JS SDK.

pricing_anchor: Meilisearch Cloud Build tier from $30/month; production tiers scale per document and per-month. See meilisearch.com/pricing.
gotchas: For a small SaaS app or a docs site, Meilisearch ships faster and the DX is genuinely best-in-class.
Meilisearch's typo tolerance and prefix search defaults are more forgiving without configuration.
JavaScript and React integration libraries are first-class and well-documented.
If you only ever do site search and have no compliance overhead, Meilisearch is hard to beat on time-to-value.
discovery_questions: What other data lives in Meilisearch today, and what is on a different stack?
Do you have enterprise IAM, audit, or compliance pressure (SOC2, ISO, FedRAMP, HIPAA)?
Is multi-tenant search a requirement, and how is isolation enforced today?
Where does observability and security telemetry live, and could one platform serve all of it?
What is the team's appetite for consolidating vendors at the next renewal?
clincher: Meilisearch wins the demo. Elastic wins the audit.

tagline: Algolia is rented relevance. Elastic is owned relevance plus the platform around it.
key_pain: Algolia ships fast, ranks well and has the best-in-class merchandising UI for product search. The cost shows up in three places: per-record-per-month pricing that punishes large catalogs, no data residency control beyond a few regions, and a ceiling at search-only when the team needs RAG, observability or security on the same data.

talking_points.claim: Per-GB ingest plus storage tiers replaces per-record-per-month at scale.
talking_points.proof: Algolia Premium lists at $1.50 per 1000 records/month; a 50M-product catalog runs into six figures monthly. Elastic indexed at the same scale runs predictable per-GB.

talking_points.claim: Elastic Cloud runs in 50+ regions across AWS, GCP and Azure, plus self-hosted and air-gapped.
talking_points.proof: Algolia hosts data in a small number of regions and does not offer self-hosted. EU, healthcare, public sector and financial customers often disqualify on residency.

talking_points.claim: Same cluster handles RAG, log analytics, observability and security.
talking_points.proof: Algolia is search-only by design. Elastic replaces multiple stacks at the next consolidation cycle.

Self-hosted, Elastic Cloud (50+ regions) and air-gapped deployments
Hybrid BM25 plus dense plus ELSER sparse with RRF
Search Applications, Behavioral Analytics and reranking included
Same data plane for site search, RAG, observability and security
Open source under AGPLv3, no full vendor lock-in

proof_points.metric: Elastic Search Applications and Behavioral Analytics ship merchandising and search KPIs natively.
Algolia Premium list price is $1.50 per 1000 records/month plus $0.50 per 1000 search requests.
Elastic Cloud is FedRAMP Moderate authorised and supports HIPAA, ISO 27001 and SOC 2.

objection_handlers.q: Algolia's merchandising and ranking UI is the best in the market.
